title: Setting your hourly rate and minimum charge for Car detailing
audience: Owners of small Australian property trade businesses who need a base rate and a minimum charge before quoting
learningOutcomes: Separate billable hours from non-billable hours, and calculate the time available to bill.
Calculate a base hourly rate from the owner's own costs and income target, then compare it with local evidence.
Set a minimum charge for short jobs, and explain it to a client before the visit.

instruction.heading: Factors that move the rate
instruction.body: A detailing rate depends on the skill and paint-correction experience you bring, how many packages you offer that a client can book in one visit, the vehicle types you take, and the cost of running a mobile or fixed set-up. A detailer who offers several packages and a clear coating option can justify a higher rate than one who offers only a wash. Do not cut the rate to win work. The research found no sourced hourly rate for car detailing. The local evidence to compare against is your own quotes, the package ranges on a Sydney vendor's list (Schmicko, modified 8 August 2026, advertised prices only) and the rates clients accept. Do not use a national average from another trade.

instruction.heading: Counting the hours that can be billed
instruction.body: Owners often price as though every hour of the week can be billed. Few can. Travel between clients, quoting, admin, marketing, bay cleaning, equipment upkeep, sick days and leave are not billable. Estimate the paid working hours in a year, subtract the non-billable time, and you have billable hours. Jobber's guide puts billable time at about 60 to 80 percent of working hours, a general range rather than an Australian figure (Jobber, 5 November 2024, modified 20 July 2026). A mobile detailer who loses time to driving, for example an illustrative 40 minutes a day, may find the billable share is at the lower end, so log one month before you rely on the range.

instruction.heading: Building the rate from costs and income
instruction.body: Add the annual costs of running the business, including insurance, registration, equipment and its upkeep, the vehicle, phone, software, marketing and accounting, to the income you need. A business.gov.au pricing guide says on-costs such as superannuation, leave and tax belong in the hourly figure, so decide how each applies to you (business.gov.au, 1 October 2026). Have a registered tax agent confirm how leave and superannuation are treated in your situation before the rate is published. Divide the total by billable hours to reach the base rate. A personal-training guide from AIPT works backwards from a target income, dividing by working weeks and then by weekly hours, with tax and business costs added on top (AIPT, 16 May 2025). Review the base rate each quarter.

instruction.heading: Setting a minimum charge for short jobs
instruction.body: A small job such as a wheel and tyre dress or a single-panel correction can cost more in time than it earns, because travel and set-up do not shrink with the job. A minimum charge covers the time to attend the site and start work. Contractor+ suggests setting a minimum from the full cost of the visit, divided by one minus the target margin, with the minimum covering travel, set-up and clean-up. Its figures are labelled illustrative and are not used here (Contractor+, 23 September 2026). Set the minimum from your own visit cost, state it before the booking, and explain it in plain terms.

instruction.heading: Price several small tasks as one visit
instruction.body: A client who books a wash, an interior clean and a glass treatment in one visit should get one labour amount, not a separate minimum for each task. Contractor+ describes pricing several small tasks in one visit as one labour amount (Contractor+, 23 September 2026). Price any extra work before you start it.

procedure: Estimate the paid working hours in a year, then subtract travel, admin, marketing, training, bay upkeep and leave to find billable hours.
List the annual running costs, including insurance, registration, equipment, vehicle, phone, software and marketing.
Add the income needed, including allowances for leave and tax confirmed by a registered tax agent.
Divide the total by billable hours to find the base rate.
Set a minimum charge that covers travel, set-up and admin for a short job, and state it in writing.
Review the rate each quarter, and record any change and the reason for it.

workedExamples.situation: A mobile detailer's log shows that about sixty of every hundred paid hours can be billed, but the owner plans to set the rate as if every paid hour could be billed.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What happens to the rate if the wrong assumption is kept?
workedExamples.reasoning: Pricing as if every paid hour were billable understates the rate. The costs and the income still have to come out of the hours that can be billed. With sixty billable hours in every hundred, the costs of all one hundred paid hours must come from the sixty, so the rate needs to be about 1.67 times the rate for a fully billable week. The rate must be built from billable hours, then checked against the package prices and the minimum charge before it is published.

workedExamples.situation: Illustrative: a detailer's short job is a single-panel paint touch-up that takes 1 hour on site, with 40 minutes of driving.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Should the hourly rate alone price this job?
workedExamples.reasoning: No. The hourly rate covers only the hour on site. The 40 minutes of driving is unpaid time under an hourly-only quote, so the effective rate is lower than the quoted one. A minimum charge that covers the drive, set-up and admin is the better answer, and it is stated before the booking.

commonErrors.error: Setting a rate from a published average or a competitor's figure without checking your own costs. Gap: no sourced car detailing rate was found.
commonErrors.prevention: Build the base rate from your own costs and billable hours, then compare it with your quotes and the local evidence you can verify.

commonErrors.error: Pricing as though every paid hour could be billed.
commonErrors.prevention: Subtract the non-billable time before dividing.

commonErrors.error: Taking short jobs at the same rate, without covering travel and set-up.
commonErrors.prevention: Set and state a minimum charge that covers travel, set-up and admin.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Price display rules come from the Australian Consumer Law, as summarised in the ACCC price display guidance (2 October 2026). That guidance says the total must include unavoidable fees. It does not settle whether a minimum or call-out charge is a fair term. Check that point with current ACCC guidance or a legal adviser before publishing a price sheet.
Confirm how leave, superannuation and tax apply to your business with a registered tax agent. This lesson gives no tax advice.

qualityStandard: Billable hours are calculated from a logged or estimated month, not assumed.
The base rate is built from the owner's costs and income target, and is compared with local evidence.
A minimum charge is set and stated before any short job.
documentationEvidence: Annual costs and income worksheet, with the source and date of each cost
Billable hours calculation showing the non-billable deductions
Price sheet showing the base rate, the minimum charge and the review date
summary: Price from billable hours, not from paid hours.
Build the rate from costs and a stated income target, then check it against your own quotes and verified local evidence.
Set and state a minimum charge for short jobs. Gap: no sourced minimum or hourly rate for car detailing was found.

knowledgeChecks.question: A detailer can bill only some of the paid hours. How should the rate be built?
options: From all paid hours, so the rate looks lower and the client pays less per job
From billable hours, so the costs and income are covered by the work that can be billed
From the average on a vendor's website and the rate listed by the nearest competitor
From the rate the owner wishes the market would pay

knowledgeChecks.question: Why set a minimum charge for a short detailing job?
options: Because a short job needs travel but no set-up time at all
Because travel, set-up and admin time does not shrink with the size of the job
Because clients expect every job to cost the same amount
Because a minimum charge replaces a written quote

knowledgeChecks.question: What is the best source for checking a base hourly rate for detailing?
options: A single published national average from another trade
Your own costs and billable hours, compared with verifiable local evidence
A friend's rate, without checking the costs or the local market
The first price shown on a bidding site this week

sourceReferences: business.gov.au, 'Choose a pricing strategy', https://business.gov.au/products-and-services/choose-a-pricing-strategy, page metadata dated 1 October 2026. Used for on-costs such as superannuation, leave and tax in the hourly figure.

Jobber, 'What are billable hours', https://getjobber.com/academy/what-are-billable-hours/, published 5 November 2024, last modified 20 July 2026. Used for the 60 to 80 percent billable range, which is a general range and not an Australian figure.

AIPT, 'Personal Training Prices: Setting the Right Rates', https://www.aipt.edu.au/articles/personal-training-prices-how-much-should-you-charge, 16 May 2025. Used for working backwards from a target income. Example figures not used.

Contractor+, 'Minimum Service Call Charge: A Contractor's Pricing Guide', https://contractorplus.app/blog/minimum-service-call-charge, 23 September 2026. Used for the minimum covering the full visit cost, and for several small tasks priced as one labour amount. The source labels its figures illustrative; not used.

Schmicko, 'Car Detailing Prices Sydney', https://schmicko.com.au/car-care/car-detailing-prices-sydney/, modified 8 August 2026. Vendor advertised prices; used only as a local reference point, not a rate.

Business Victoria, 'Develop a pricing strategy', https://business.vic.gov.au/business-information/finance/pricing-for-profit/develop-a-pricing-strategy, no date shown. Used for reviewing prices about every three months.

officialReferences.title: Price displays (ACCC)
officialReferences.covers: States that the total price must include unavoidable fees, shown as a single figure. Does not address minimum or call-out charges, or tax on leave and superannuation, which remain unconfirmed. Publisher: ACCC.
